segments.voice: Then two weeks of the peace chants, and last week closed on purnam adah: take the full from the full, and the full remains. Today's chant starts at the ears.

The alarm. A headline. Someone's mood through the bedroom wall. All of it got in before the first decision of the day, before anyone chose it. Now a different morning, long ago. A few students sit down with their teacher to study the Mundaka, or the Prashna, or the Mandukya. The text is right there. But before a word of it, the whole room says something else first, together: O gods, may we hear with our ears what is good.
screen: `IT GOT IN BEFORE YOU CHOSE.` → `A ROOM, BEFORE THE TEXT.` → `MAY WE HEAR WHAT IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: The chant is known by its first words, bhadram karnebhih. Its lines come from a hymn of the Rig Veda, and tradition chants it with those three Upanishads. In plain words: O gods, may we hear with our ears what is good. May we see with our eyes what is good. With steady limbs and bodies, praising you, may we live out the span the gods have set. Then a second verse asks well-being from four names: Indra, Pushan who knows all, Tarkshya, and Brihaspati. And then: Om, peace, peace, peace. Look at the order. Ears first, then eyes, then a steady body, then a full life. The Upanishads that follow ask the hardest questions there are about the self. But this chant doesn't begin with the self. It begins with the senses, the doors everything comes through. Bhadram means good, auspicious, the kind of thing that does a person well. Before the big questions, the students ask that what passes through those doors be bhadram. And the request is plural: may we hear, may we see. The whole room asks together, just as it did in saha navavatu.
screen: `BHADRAM: GOOD, AUSPICIOUS.` · `EARS, EYES, A STEADY BODY.` · `THE SENSES ARE THE DOORS.` · then, large: `MAY WE HEAR WHAT IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Let sounds arrive on their own, near ones and far ones, and for each, simply notice that it came in through the ears. Don't judge them. Near the end, choose one sound that does you good, even your own breath, and stay with it.
The peace chants, and today bhadram karnebhih: may we hear with our ears what is good, and see with our eyes what is good.
To carry: then two weeks of the peace chants and the closing mantras of each Upanishad, ears first, then eyes. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: your little brother falls asleep to videos that leave him wired and scared. by bhadram karnebhih, what's a good first move?
options: help him choose what reaches his ears before he sleeps.
nothing; what comes in through the ears doesn't change anyone.
take every screen away for good; sound is the enemy of rest.
fork.reveal: the chant doesn't ask for silence. it asks that what comes in through the ears and eyes be good.

chat.says: finals week and the class group chat is pure gossip about a teacher 🙄 is muting it rude?
options: not rude. the chant's first ask is that what comes in through the ears be good.
rude; you have to hear all of it, or you're just hiding from real life.
keep reading; the chant only asks for good sounds inside a temple.
chat.meaning: Bhadram karnebhih begins with the senses: may we hear with our ears what is good. Choosing what comes in isn't rude.

bhadram.meaning: good, auspicious: what does a person well
